title: Last time he saw his father play, a funeral, and funerals with bands
summary: Arthur remembers father on bass drum at a funeral, Catholic funerals with bands, and bands for Sidney's funeral; he was the eighth of nine children.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: The last time I remember seeing my father play, there was an old fellow playing, had died, and he was playing a funeral. And we was there, I was standing right in the avenue out on Clever Street, and the funeral would pass, and some part of the island, they used to call him Jean Vigne, that was the name they called him for the name, they wouldn't say Jean, they used to say Jean Vigne.
That's what I heard that name, that's what I thought might be in French.

Yeah, Jean Vigne is how they used to call me, because they were mostly like in French, you know, and when they called him, when they hollered at him, he said, I'm going to hit four more licks on this guy, he said, because someday he'll hit four on mine. And that's the last time I could remember of him playing music, you know, that I remember hearing him play. And he was beating the bass drum at the time. Yeah. And after that funeral, in fact, my brother was just older than me, we followed the funeral all the way to St. Louis graveyard. And after they got through, Baron, the man that was coming back playing, didn't he ramble, and they was carrying on him, and that was really the last time I could remember my father playing music. And then later on, he got sick, and a year later he was dead. But I don't remember the name of the band he was with when he played at the funeral, I don't remember that so well.
You remember when he died, did they have a band for his funeral too? Oh yeah.
Oh yeah. Were you all Catholics, I suppose? Catholics, yeah, we were Catholics.
At present, I don't usually, the Catholics don't favor having bands on the street for their funerals, but I just wanted to know that they did.

As of now they don't. They don't approve of it too much now. But in them times they did. They did a fun other day. Yeah, they're Catholic, they went with bands. And if they didn't want to have the band, well then they would just have the priest to bless the body at the house. And they'd go right to the graveyard. That's right. Yeah. If they didn't want to, if they just want, now my brother Sidney got killed, they might have had about seven bands behind him. Because any time a musician had died, they'd always have a band behind him. Because sometimes the wife didn't want it, didn't approve of it, you see. But most of the time they would let it go through because they knew that was his life, music and they just let music carry him away. But my father had music, I remember that well. He had maybe about two or three bands behind him. My brother had about five. He had so many of them behind him. I remember far back you could see, you could hear bands one after the other. He had a trouble as I was night, my brother Sidney was living. Oh babe, they could tell you a lot about it. Because they were, you see we have, I have about, let's see. One, two, three, four, five, six. I have about six in between my brother Sidney and I, that's how much older they were. You see if they were living, they'd be around in the, my brother Sidney would be in his seventies now if he was living. You see, yeah. And I mean they could remember everything because they were, I mean boys were big enough to be around my daddy a lot before he died around his music and all. You know they could tell you a lot about it. Then my brother played music but I was next to the baby, you see. We were nine children and I was the eighth one. So I mean that made me be real young over there under them, you see. And that's why they would know so much more than I would. Even my sisters would know more, my older sisters. But right now I got one sister older than me and she was crippled, she never did go anywhere. So I knew she wouldn't know too much. She was always home, you know she had, her hip was hurting, she used to limp and she never did go anywhere but stay in the house. So she's the only one, the only three left now and she's the only one that would be old enough to know anything. She didn't go anywhere by being crippled.

I was trying to figure if your father were living, he'd be about a hundred years old I guess. In his nineties then. Yeah. He died forty, I don't know, forty five years ago. He doesn't look close to a hundred then, wasn't he?

Yeah he would, he would. Because he died when he was around, up in his fifties. And he was dead a good forty five years ago. Because my daddy died when I was only thirteen year old. And I know that's a good forty five years ago. Because I'm fifty eight now.
